Diagnostic check: Before answering, identify bonding and particle structure: ionic crystal/network vs separate covalent units; ask whether a single formula unit exists independently.
Use when: Apply this to chemistry questions contrasting compounds or substances by particle type, bonding, or whether “molecules” are present.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about macroscopic form, mixtures, metallic solids, or exceptions requiring crystal-structure detail beyond basic bonding class.

Transfer rule: If two materials share composition but belong to different rock classes, then classify by formation process, not by ingredients.
Error pattern: Success comes from prioritizing defining criteria over superficial sameness in content.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is this category defined by how it forms, when it forms, or what it contains?” and choose the defining basis.
Use when: Apply this to Earth science classification questions comparing igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic materials with similar chemistry.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly asks about composition, age, fossils, or another stated property rather than classification basis.

Transfer rule: If asked to determine mass, then choose the instrument that directly measures mass, not one for holding, transferring, or measuring volume.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the target quantity to the tool’s primary function instead of being distracted by the material or container.
Diagnostic check: Underline the quantity named; ask “Which option outputs that quantity directly?” and reject tools used only to contain, move, or size samples.
Use when: Apply on basic lab-equipment multiple choice where several familiar tools appear and only one matches the requested measurement type.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for preparation, transfer, heating, observation, or when a tool measures indirectly through a stated procedure.

Transfer rule: If a unit is defined by an Earth–Sun average distance, then prefer pairs of objects within the same planetary system scale, not stars, constellations, or galaxies.
Error pattern: I matched a space-related term to the largest astronomical scale instead of the scale implied by the unit’s definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option by scale—planetary, interstellar, or galactic—and eliminate every choice not on the unit’s native scale.
Use when: The question asks which situations a scientific unit is most often used for and the unit’s definition names a reference distance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the unit is explicitly for extreme scales or the problem asks for unusual, nonstandard usage.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about new star formation, then favor processes involving interstellar gas and dust collecting into dense clouds, often enriched by matter from older dead stars.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the life-cycle stage to recycled material accumulation rather than choosing processes tied to late-stage stellar evolution or mature stellar cores.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as birth-stage, main-sequence-stage, or death-stage; keep only choices that increase nebular mass and collapse potential.
Use when: Apply this on astronomy items about how stars begin, nebulae, protostars, or the stellar life cycle.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about what happens inside an already formed star or its end-state remnant.

Transfer rule: If asked which stage returns water from the atmosphere to land, then choose the stage where water falls to Earth’s surface.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking process direction through the system rather than matching familiar vocabulary loosely.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark source and destination; select only the one with atmosphere → ground/soil.
Use when: Apply on cycle-process questions with several named stages that differ mainly by movement direction or location.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about cloud formation, upward movement, plant release, or storage instead of return to soil.

Transfer rule: If a classification question lists traits, then test each candidate group against every trait and keep groups that can satisfy all of them, even if not typically.
Error pattern: Success came from eliminating groups by incompatible hallmark traits while allowing broad groups with diverse members.
Diagnostic check: Make a trait-by-group grid; for each group, mark yes/no for each trait, then verify no excluded group actually has exceptions.
Use when: This fits taxonomy or category questions using a short set of biological characteristics to identify possible groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a single specific organism, molecular detail, or a rule with no meaningful within-group variation.

Transfer rule: If a species is described as thriving in a specific habitat condition, then choose the environmental change that most strongly removes that condition for the longest time.
Error pattern: Correct pattern: matching an organism’s stated resource dependence to the option that creates the clearest sustained resource shortage.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the key habitat need, then test each option for whether it increases, decreases, or barely affects that need, prioritizing duration and directness.
Use when: Apply this on ecology questions describing where an organism grows best, survives best, or is specially adapted to.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question hinges on predators, competition, disease, or life-cycle timing rather than habitat-resource availability.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how a beneficial inherited trait could change descendants, then choose the outcome where that trait improves survival/reproduction and becomes more common over generations.
Error pattern: Success pattern: applying natural selection correctly instead of confusing it with mutation rate changes, unrelated harm, or immediate extinction.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the trait heritable, does it plausibly help getting food/avoiding danger, and does the option describe gradual population change across generations?
Use when: Use for evolution questions about one organism’s advantageous variation affecting later descendants or a population over time.
Boundary: Ignore when the trait is not inherited, the timescale is individual lifetime only, or the question is about development rather than selection.

Transfer rule: If a reaction seems to lose mass, then first check for open-system loss or measurement limits before invoking mass-energy changes or volume effects.
Error pattern: Treated dramatic or irrelevant mechanisms as plausible instead of prioritizing ordinary experimental causes consistent with conservation laws.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Could material leave the container? Could instrument resolution, calibration, or reading uncertainty explain the difference? Reject explanations that do not change total mass.
Use when: Comparing reactant and product mass in lab reactions, especially with repeated small discrepancies and proposed explanations of observed mass differences.
Boundary: Ignore when the setup is explicitly closed and high-precision data or nuclear-scale processes are specified.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where sunlight is least intense on a solstice date, then compare hemisphere tilt and pick the place tilted most away from the Sun.  
Error pattern: Success came from using Earth’s axial tilt and season geometry instead of surface temperature or latitude alone.  
Diagnostic check: First identify the date’s solstice/equinox, then mark which hemisphere is tilted away, then rank choices by how far into that dark-tilted region they are.  
Use when: This applies to questions about sunlight intensity, day length, or solar angle by location and time of year.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem depends on clouds, altitude, local weather, or asks about heat rather than incoming sunlight.

Transfer rule: If conditions change only the local gravitational field, then predict a change in weight, not in intrinsic body properties.
Error pattern: Success came from separating location-dependent quantities from object-dependent quantities.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each candidate as “depends on gravity” or “depends on the object itself” and choose only gravity-dependent ones.
Use when: Apply this to questions comparing the same person or object across planets, moons, elevators, or changing gravity levels.
Boundary: Ignore this when the object’s composition, amount of matter, shape, or external forces besides gravity are also changing.

Transfer rule: If tracing a wind-causing process from solar input, then order the transfers as incoming radiation, surface-to-air conduction, then rising-air convection before motion.
Error pattern: Success came from following the physical chain step by step instead of jumping from solar heating directly to moving air.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each arrow to a specific location: Sun to ground, ground to nearby air, warm air rising/cool air sinking, then horizontal air movement.
Use when: Apply this to questions about heating-driven air movement, density changes, land-water temperature differences, or atmospheric circulation sequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the process is not solar-heating-driven or when transfer occurs mainly through direct contact without bulk fluid motion.

Transfer rule: If identifying a biological group by trait, then choose the defining body-plan feature shared across the group, not a common but nonuniversal covering or appendage.
Error pattern: Mistook a familiar outward trait for the diagnostic anatomical hallmark.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is this trait fundamental to the group’s body organization and broadly present, including forms lacking protective coverings?”
Use when: Classification questions ask which characteristic identifies members of an animal phylum or broad taxonomic group from several plausible traits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets a specific subgroup, life stage, or an exception-focused habitat adaptation rather than phylum-level identification.

Transfer rule: If options compare energy resources by pollution, then rank them by full lifecycle emissions and direct combustion waste before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from applying domain knowledge instead of surface cues or popularity of “green” resources.
Diagnostic check: Ask: which option requires burning fuel and releases the largest air pollutants and greenhouse gases during normal use?
Use when: This fits multiple-choice questions contrasting power sources, fuels, or technologies on environmental harm or emissions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets cost, reliability, land use, manufacturing impacts only, or a specific pollutant not total pollution.

Transfer rule: If data are paired value conversions or exact lookup results, then present them in a table for the clearest reference.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the representation to the task: precise comparison and retrieval beat trend or part-to-whole displays.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Will the audience need exact matched entries more than trends, proportions, or a calculation rule?” If yes, choose a table.
Use when: The problem gives two corresponding quantities across many cases and asks for the clearest way to show the converted information.
Boundary: Ignore this when the goal is showing change over time, category shares, or generating outputs from a general relationship.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for environmental effects, then choose the option about impacts on living organisms or ecosystems, not cost, schedule, materials, or human amenities.
Error pattern: Success came from separating ecological consequences from logistical or recreational details.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option as ecosystem impact, construction detail, economic factor, or human use; select only from ecosystem-impact choices.
Use when: Apply this on public works, land-use, water-control, or infrastructure questions asking for environmental importance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt instead asks about engineering feasibility, budgeting, timelines, or social benefits rather than environmental effects.

Transfer rule: If asked which factors most affect river health, then prioritize direct water-quality indicators that immediately alter oxygen, light, and organism stress over broader background conditions.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting proximate ecological drivers rather than indirect, intermittent, or context-dependent influences.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this factor directly change water clarity, nutrient loading, or chemical conditions in ways that quickly affect aquatic life?
Use when: Apply this on environmental multiple-choice items comparing variables by how strongly and directly they impact ecosystem health.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets geology, long-term watershed formation, or a specific local case where indirect factors dominate.

Transfer rule: If choices mix universal matter terms with a basic life-specific structure, then select the feature unique to organisms.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing traits shared by all matter from traits exclusive to living systems.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: can a rock, water, or air sample also have this? Eliminate any option answered yes.
Use when: The question asks for a defining difference between living and nonliving things using introductory science vocabulary.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about processes, exceptions, or advanced cases like viruses, seeds, or dormant states.

Transfer rule: If asked for an acquired trait, then choose a behavior shaped by use, learning, or interaction with surroundings, not a built-in reflex or basic need response.
Error pattern: Mistaking a temporary location or situation-dependent action for a lasting environmentally developed behavior.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Would this likely appear without experience, or does repeated contact/practice trigger it?” Reject mere posture/place choices.
Use when: Relevant in biology questions contrasting inherited behaviors with traits or habits influenced by environment, experience, or physical interaction.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when options compare only body structures, or when all behaviors are clearly innate reflexes or species-typical signals.

Transfer rule: If organisms share the same limited soil resources in one area, then choose the option about competition reducing the desired organism’s growth.
Error pattern: Success came from applying ecological competition instead of selecting effects that are indirect, exaggerated, or beneficial.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the shared limiting resources both organisms need; if both require them, prefer the choice describing resource competition.
Use when: A question involves plants growing together, one being removed, and asks for the most likely biological reason.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives evidence about disease control, physical obstruction, chemical treatment, or a specifically stated alternative mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what rises when offspring count rises, then prefer population-level odds over per-offspring benefits.
Error pattern: Success came from separating total reproductive payoff from individual growth, care, or resources.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: would this usually increase, decrease, or stay limited as brood size grows under finite parental resources?
Use when: Apply this to life-history, evolution, or ecology items about tradeoffs between litter size and offspring outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives abundant resources, cooperative care, or a direct mechanism boosting each offspring equally.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which observation does not support past continental connection, then prefer evidence requiring former land contact, not present-day ocean similarity.
Error pattern: I treated a classic direct fit clue as weak and overlooked that marine distribution can result from existing ocean continuity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this still occur even if the continents had never been joined?” Eliminate any option answerable yes.
Use when: Apply on Earth science items about continental drift, fossils, rock strata, coastline fit, or species distributions across separated regions.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt concerns ocean currents, modern migration, climate matching, or asks for strongest rather than non-supporting evidence.

Transfer rule: If motion is vertical near Earth with negligible air resistance, then apply constant downward acceleration to infer speed changes over time.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking acceleration’s direction instead of assuming speed stays constant except at a turning point.
Diagnostic check: Mark three moments—upward travel, highest point, downward travel—and verify speed decreases, reaches zero briefly, then increases.
Use when: Relevant for one-dimensional motion under gravity, especially “thrown up and comes down” descriptions asking about speed behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when strong drag, propulsion, bouncing, or nonvertical paths make acceleration nonconstant or not purely downward.

Transfer rule: If one option uniquely combines freezing surface temperatures with strong winds and substantial frozen precipitation, then choose that option.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the full condition set, not latching onto only wind or only severe-storm intensity.
Diagnostic check: List each required trait; eliminate any choice missing one, especially below-freezing air at the surface and precipitation type.
Use when: Apply on multiple-choice weather questions that ask for an event defined by a specific bundle of atmospheric conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about rare exceptions, regional variants, or impacts rather than the standard defining conditions.

Transfer rule: If a developmental change weakens an adult courtship or display behavior, then infer reduced mating success and lower reproductive fitness.
Error pattern: Success came from linking an immediate behavioral deficit to its direct evolutionary consequence, not to unrelated survival or resource effects.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is the impaired trait mainly used to attract partners or compete for reproduction?” If yes, prioritize mating consequences.
Use when: A stem describes poorer singing, displays, ornaments, or other sexual-signaling behaviors caused by stress, development, or condition.
Boundary: Ignore this when the trait is explicitly tied to feeding, predator avoidance, thermoregulation, or territory acquisition rather than courtship.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what contributes to seasonal daylight and temperature changes, then choose the planet’s yearly orbit as the needed motion, while remembering tilt explains the pattern.
Error pattern: Success came from linking seasons to annual position-related sunlight changes rather than daily spinning, changing solar output, or simple distance claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each cause by asking: does it produce a year-long cycle in both daylight length and sun angle across regions?
Use when: Apply this on astronomy items contrasting daily motion, yearly motion, sunlight intensity, and seasonal climate or daylight differences.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is specifically about day/night, time zones, sunrise timing within a day, or tides.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which human action caused a measured environmental change, then choose the action with a plausible physical mechanism linking it to that specific variable.
Error pattern: Success came from causal-mechanism matching rather than picking any human activity merely associated with the location.
Diagnostic check: For each option, state a one-step chain “action → process → measured change”; eliminate options that lack a direct, credible pathway.
Use when: Environmental science items ask about human impacts on water, air, habitat, or chemistry and provide several activities or events.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for historical facts, definitions, or when causation is explicitly given and no mechanism inference is needed.

Transfer rule: If a substance spreads on its own from where it is concentrated into surrounding material until evenly mixed, then choose the particle-spreading process.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the observable mixing behavior to the mechanism based on concentration differences, not unrelated transport or wearing-away terms.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is there passive movement from high concentration to low concentration within a fluid, with no membrane, blood transfer, or surface breakdown involved?”
Use when: Apply for scenarios about drops, smells, gases, or dissolved particles gradually dispersing through air or liquid over time.
Boundary: Ignore when the change involves membranes, bulk flow by pumping, transfer between organisms, or physical removal of material from a surface.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a technology is primarily designed to do versus a conventional counterpart, then pick the main engineering goal, not an absolute or side benefit.
Error pattern: Success comes from distinguishing core design purpose from exaggerated outcomes and unrelated performance traits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare each option against standard design tradeoffs: efficiency, power, emissions, and fuel dependence; reject choices claiming total elimination or independence unless the technology inherently allows it.
Use when: Apply this to comparative questions about vehicles, energy systems, or devices with mixed power sources.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about a specific model’s feature, a regulatory outcome, or a nonprimary secondary effect.

Transfer rule: If a classification item lists ectothermy plus egg-laying, then first match the broad animal group defined by those core traits before considering rarer extras.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing high-diagnostic, category-level traits and treating unusual features as supporting, not decisive.
Diagnostic check: Make a two-column trait screen: backbone/animal vs microbe, warm- vs cold-regulated, live birth vs eggs, feathers/fur/scales; choose the group matching the most defining traits.
Use when: Apply this on life-science multiple choice asking for organism groups from several physical or reproductive descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for species-level identification or when key traits are missing, contradictory, or about habitat alone.

Transfer rule: If a category includes both elements and compounds, then choose the definition based on fixed composition, not composition type or physical state.
Error pattern: Success came from testing each option against all examples instead of matching a single familiar case.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the statement holds for an element, a compound, and different room-temperature states; reject any claim failing one case.
Use when: Relevant for classification questions about substances, matter types, or definitions that must include multiple kinds of examples.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about only elements, only compounds, or a specific substance’s properties.

Transfer rule: If distance is given and the question asks for speed, then identify the missing quantity needed for speed = distance ÷ time.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the target quantity to its defining formula instead of choosing distracting but irrelevant measurements.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the formula for the asked-for quantity and verify which variable is not already provided.
Use when: This applies to rate, speed, density, or other formula-based questions that mix one essential input with unrelated facts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a different quantity, gives all formula inputs already, or requires a non-formula concept.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the likely effect of removing a major ecosystem component, then trace direct ecological consequences first.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing the immediate system impact rather than an appealing but opposite secondary claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list two direct functions the removed organism provides; eliminate choices that predict increases in those functions after removal.
Use when: Apply this to environmental cause-effect items about habitat, vegetation removal, pollution, erosion, oxygen, or food webs.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns short-term human management, artificial replacements, or a specific exception stated in the question.

Transfer rule: If asked which process makes carbon available in the atmosphere, then choose a process that releases stored carbon as gas, not one that stores or uses it.
Error pattern: Confusing carbon uptake or long-term storage steps with carbon-release steps in the carbon cycle.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does this move carbon into the air immediately?” Eliminate any process that removes atmospheric carbon or locks it into biomass, soil, or rock.
Use when: Relevant in cycle questions about reservoirs, fluxes, combustion, decay, respiration, burial, or uptake.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about carbon fixation, sequestration, underground storage, or long-term formation processes.

Transfer rule: If asked for evidence of constant cell division, then prefer a directly observable, ongoing cell loss or replacement process over unrelated body functions or needs.
Error pattern: Success comes from linking the claim to direct turnover evidence, not to metabolism, organ variety, or general activity.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does this phenomenon require new cells to continuously replace lost ones, rather than merely showing energy use or structure?
Use when: Relevant in biology questions about growth, repair, maintenance, tissue renewal, or identifying evidence for mitosis in everyday body processes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about causes of cell division, specialized exceptions, or nonhuman systems without routine tissue turnover.

Transfer rule: If a celestial body moves farther away, then first trace how reduced gravity weakens the effect it directly causes on another body.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing the nearest causal mechanism instead of indirect or unrelated astronomical changes.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which option changes immediately from weaker gravitational force?” Eliminate choices needing extra assumptions or different systems.
Use when: Relevant in astronomy questions about changing distance, gravity, tides, or orbital interactions between two bodies.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem centers on light, atmosphere, geology, or a stated mechanism other than gravitational influence.

Transfer rule: If two objects differ in height by only a tiny amount compared with the planet’s radius, then treat gravitational force on them as essentially the same.
Error pattern: Success comes from comparing the scale that gravity depends on to the small change described, rather than focusing on energy or lifting effort.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does the force depend mainly on mass and distance to the planet’s center, and is the distance change negligible relative to that radius?”
Use when: Use for questions about weight or gravity at slightly different elevations near a planet’s surface.
Boundary: Ignore when altitude changes are large, another massive body matters, or the question is about work or potential energy instead of force.

Transfer rule: If a problem asks to improve a material property, then change the material to one with that property rather than altering size, amount, or another sample of the same material.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the failure mode to the underlying material property instead of being distracted by superficial design changes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option change the substance itself, or only its dimensions, thickness, or source?”
Use when: Apply this on questions about durability, hardness, scratching, denting, strength, flexibility, or similar physical properties of objects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the property depends mainly on shape, dimensions, structure, or processing rather than the material type.

Transfer rule: If samples are the same substance, then rank thermal energy by combining amount present with temperature; larger amount and higher temperature means more.
Error pattern: Success pattern—used the correct two-variable comparison instead of focusing on only one feature.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, make a 2-column scan: identify which sample has the greatest amount and which has the greatest temperature; if one sample leads in both, choose it.
Use when: Relevant for comparing thermal energy, heat content, or internal energy among samples of the same material with given sizes and temperatures.
Boundary: Ignore this when substances differ, phase changes matter, or the question asks about temperature alone rather than total thermal energy.

Transfer rule: If asked for a feature that distinguishes one cell type, then choose the function tied to an organelle unique to that type, not a shared life process.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering out universal cell functions and matching the remaining choice to a type-specific structure-function pair.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: do both cell types perform this? If yes, eliminate it; keep only functions requiring a unique organelle.
Use when: Apply on biology comparisons between cell types, organisms, or structures where one option is a common process and another depends on specialized anatomy.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about structures, exceptions, or nonstandard cases rather than the usual distinguishing function.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a by-product of a metabolic process, then separate required inputs from released outputs.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying process components by role rather than matching familiar biology words.
Diagnostic check: List the process’s main input materials and output materials; choose only something released but not reused as a reactant.
Use when: Apply this to life-science questions about respiration, photosynthesis, digestion, or other transformations with inputs and outputs.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about structures, functions, definitions, or regulatory steps rather than process products.

Transfer rule: If a process shows reaction with the surroundings that creates a new substance, then classify it as a chemical change; otherwise treat shape, size, or state changes as physical.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing composition change from mere form or phase change.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Afterward, is it still the same substance?” Test for clues like color change from air exposure, corrosion, gas, precipitate, odor, or hard-to-reverse change.
Use when: Apply on multiple-choice items contrasting melting, bending, hammering, grinding, dissolving, or heating against signs of reaction.
Boundary: Ignore this shortcut when the prompt indicates only a temporary appearance change, lighting effect, or a physical mixing/state change without new substances.

Transfer rule: If asked what changes sound speed, then choose properties of the medium, not features of the wave or how it was produced.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning distinguishes medium-dependent propagation from source-dependent or wave-measure descriptions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, sort each choice into medium property, wave property, or source property; only the first can set propagation speed in a given condition.
Use when: Apply for conceptual questions about mechanical-wave speed, especially when options mix material type with amplitude, wavelength, or cause of motion.
Boundary: Ignore when the question changes conditions like temperature or asks about frequency, energy, or relationships after speed is already specified.

Transfer rule: If a mixing question asks which pair forms a new substance, then choose the pair that undergoes a reaction with observable products, not mere blending or dissolving.
Error pattern: Success comes from distinguishing chemical change from physical combination by evidence of substance formation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: after combining, do signs like gas, temperature change, precipitate, color change, or hard-to-reverse transformation appear?
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items contrasting mixtures, dissolving, or simple contact with reactive combinations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is only about separability, state changes, or no evidence of reaction is available.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how many cycles fit into a larger cycle, then estimate by dividing the larger period by the smaller and choose the nearest plausible option.
Error pattern: Success came from using rate/period comparison, but a risk is sloppy rounding after getting a quotient between choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute rough periods, divide, and verify the result is closest to one option and not off by more than about half a cycle.
Use when: Apply this to astronomy, calendars, rotations, or any repeated-motion problem comparing counts within a fixed time span.
Boundary: Ignore this when periods vary significantly, the motion is nonperiodic, or the question asks for an exact value from a specific definition.

Transfer rule: If asked to identify a state of matter, then match each option to particle behavior and choose the one with a fixed shape and volume.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying examples by physical state rather than by where they occur or how they move.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does it keep its own shape without a container, flow to fit a container, or spread out to fill space?
Use when: This applies to basic science questions that describe everyday forms of a substance or weather events.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on temperature change, mixed states, or unusual materials with nonstandard behavior.

Transfer rule: If asked which tool best separates a solid mixed with a liquid, then choose a device that physically retains particles while letting the liquid pass.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the tool’s function to the task, not to measuring, observing, or weighing.
Diagnostic check: State the mixture’s two components, then ask of each option: does it directly create separation, or only measure/view/compare?
Use when: Apply this on questions about mixtures, materials, or lab tools where the goal is to isolate one substance from another.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not separation, or when the solid is dissolved so particle-trapping will not work.

Transfer rule: If asked for a “highly reactive metal,” then first eliminate nonmetals and noble gases, then compare remaining metals by typical group reactivity and choose the best fit offered.
Error pattern: Success came from process-of-elimination, but with overthinking about an ideal category match instead of selecting the strongest available match.
Diagnostic check: List each option as metal/nonmetal/noble gas; if only one plausible reactive metal remains, pick it without requiring a perfect textbook example.
Use when: Relevant for periodic-table multiple choice questions about reactivity, families, or identifying metals versus nonmetals from element names or symbols.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the most reactive overall element, a specific group member, or gives compounds/ions instead of elemental choices.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what kind of energy is stored in a material or fuel, then identify the energy in its internal bonds, not the energy released after use.
Error pattern: Success comes from classifying energy by storage mechanism; failures usually confuse stored energy with motion, emitted waves, or atomic-origin energy.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the energy contained in molecular bonds of the substance?” If yes, choose the bond-based category.
Use when: Apply this to fuels, food, batteries, and other substances described as storing energy before being used or burned.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about energy during movement, light/heat being emitted, or changes in the atomic nucleus.

Transfer rule: If a habitat’s continued support for native organisms is asked, then choose the action that preserves existing conditions with minimal human disturbance.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a conservation principle: ecosystems persist best when their key physical conditions are not altered.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking, “Would this change water levels, land structure, or human use in a way that disrupts current species?”
Use when: Apply this on ecology questions about maintaining habitats, biodiversity, or survival of resident plants and animals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about restoration after damage, active management of invasives, or species that require deliberate intervention.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what stays the same during a physical change, then check which conserved quantity remains unchanged despite changes in form.
Error pattern: Success comes from distinguishing conserved properties from variables that commonly shift during phase changes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list matter amount, occupied space, thermal condition, and phase; mark which can change during melting while the amount of substance stays constant.
Use when: Apply this to scenarios involving melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, or reshaping the same material in a closed setting.
Boundary: Ignore this when material is added, removed, spilled, evaporates away, reacts chemically, or the system is not closed.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what fills a visible bubble, then identify the trapped gas inside rather than the liquid film making the shell.
Error pattern: Success came from separating container material from contents and choosing the interior substance, not the surrounding membrane.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label “shell” versus “inside”; ask which part occupies the center volume enclosed by the thin film.
Use when: Apply to everyday physical objects with a coating, wrapper, bubble, shell, or container surrounding something else.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about the wall material, dissolved components, or cases where the interior is intentionally specified otherwise.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why one celestial object appears brighter, then compare apparent brightness by distance first, not by size alone.
Error pattern: Success came from using apparent-observation reasoning rather than assuming intrinsic properties determine what looks brightest from Earth.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Are these objects viewed from different distances?” If yes, test whether closeness alone explains the observed brightness.
Use when: Relevant for astronomy items about how bright, large, or visible objects appear from an observer’s location.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about actual energy output, physical size, or when distances are stated equal or negligible.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what rock forms when molten material cools and hardens, then choose the rock type produced by solidification.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a process description to the defining formation mechanism of a rock category.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the sequence in words: molten material → cooling/solidifying; verify the option names a rock formed by that process.
Use when: Apply this on Earth science items about rock-cycle processes, especially eruption, lava, magma, cooling, or hardening clues.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about the molten material itself, altered existing rock, or rock formed from compacted sediments.

Transfer rule: If motion changes speed after moving from one surface to another, then identify whether the net force has become nonzero rather than focusing on gravity alone.
Error pattern: Success came from checking balanced versus unbalanced forces using the observed change in motion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the object’s speed and direction constant?” If not, conclude forces are unbalanced; if yes, conclude they are balanced.
Use when: Apply this to mechanics questions linking changes in speed or direction to force explanations across ramps, flats, or surface transitions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a specific force’s magnitude or direction instead of the net-force condition.

Transfer rule: If a climate question compares heating by latitude, then choose the cause based on sunlight angle and energy concentration, not distance, speed, or unrelated geography.
Error pattern: Mixing a correct mechanism with a false supporting reason; the answer may be right while the justification uses a common misconception.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: does this cause directly change incoming solar intensity per area over the year, and would it still work if Earth–Sun distance were nearly constant?
Use when: Apply for Earth science items about seasons, temperature zones, ocean heating, or why equatorial regions are warmer than polar regions.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem is about local currents, altitude, albedo, atmospheric effects, or short-term weather rather than latitude-driven insolation.

Transfer rule: If land vegetation is removed, then predict exposed-soil effects: more erosion, nutrient loss, and reduced soil quality rather than ecosystem gains.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing direct ecological consequences of removing plant cover and rejecting choices that claim opposite-direction benefits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare each option to a quick chain: fewer roots/canopy -> less soil protection/moisture retention -> more runoff/leaching -> lower topsoil fertility.
Use when: Apply on environmental cause-effect questions about deforestation, habitat loss, vegetation removal, erosion, nutrient cycling, or atmospheric impacts.
Boundary: Ignore when the scenario includes restoration, sustainable management, short-term crop yield, or engineered controls that offset normal soil-loss effects.

Transfer rule: If heat transfer occurs within a liquid or gas because the material itself circulates, then classify it as convection.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the mechanism to moving fluid rather than to mere contact or direct heating.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does the warmed substance flow and carry energy to cooler regions?” If yes, convection is the likely category.
Use when: Apply this on questions contrasting conduction, convection, and radiation in situations involving liquids, gases, or bulk motion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for heat transfer mainly through solids, electromagnetic emission, or where no fluid movement is described.

Transfer rule: If a process in a cycle moves water from sea to atmosphere, then identify the phase/separation step and track what impurities are left behind.  
Error pattern: Confusing a location change with the wrong state change instead of checking which properties are conserved or filtered out.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list start state, end state, phase at each stage, and whether dissolved materials travel with the vapor.  
Use when: Relevant for water-cycle, phase-change, purification, evaporation, condensation, or dissolved-substance questions.  
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about freezing, melting, sublimation, chemical reactions, or energy changes without separation of dissolved materials.

Transfer rule: If a climate question asks for the direct cause of low rainfall, then choose the option about immediate atmospheric moisture supply before geographic proxies.
Error pattern: I over-weighted an indirect correlate and skipped the nearer causal mechanism controlling precipitation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which choice names the thing clouds/rain physically require?”; if one option states moisture availability, prefer it over location descriptors.
Use when: This applies to weather or climate items contrasting physical precipitation ingredients with broad map-position facts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt specifically asks for an indirect regional driver, transport pathway, or topographic cause.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the first stage in a named geologic sequence, then reconstruct the full sequence and pick the earliest event.
Error pattern: Success came from ordering related processes instead of choosing by familiarity or by which step directly forms the final material.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the stages in order from source-material breakdown through movement, settling, squeezing, and mineral binding; confirm which comes first.
Use when: Apply this to Earth science items about process sequences, cycles, or rock formation stages with several plausible consecutive steps.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a later stage, a definition, a cause rather than an order, or a sequence from a different system.

Transfer rule: If a choice states a pure substance made from multiple elements can exist as single atoms, then reject it as a valid compound description.
Error pattern: Success came from checking each definition against particle-level structure rather than relying on familiar wording.
Diagnostic check: Ask: must this substance include at least two different elements chemically bonded, and can an isolated single atom satisfy that? If yes, the statement is false.
Use when: The item asks for the statement that is not true about compounds, elements, molecules, or methods of separation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns ions, mixtures, network solids, or exceptions outside basic introductory definitions.

Transfer rule: If options mix sudden hazards with a gradual earth process, then choose the one requiring the longest accumulation before measurable change.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing timescales instead of focusing on drama, visibility, or destruction.
Diagnostic check: Classify each option as instant, short-duration, or cumulative; pick the cumulative process only if its effects build over many repeated events.
Use when: This applies to science questions asking which phenomenon takes the longest time to produce observable environmental change.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about immediate impact, single-event magnitude, or human-accelerated rates rather than natural timescale.

Transfer rule: If one option forms a new substance through reaction, then choose it over options showing only changes of state, shape, or appearance.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing composition change from physical rearrangement using substance identity, not surface-level descriptiveness.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “After the change, is the material chemically different and not easily reversed by simple physical means?”
Use when: Apply on classification questions contrasting physical and chemical changes in everyday materials or processes.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on energy transfer, biological labeling, or mixed processes where evidence for new substance formation is missing.

Transfer rule: If choosing a scientific hypothesis, then select a testable cause-and-effect statement about the suspected variable and outcome.
Error pattern: Success comes from preferring investigable mechanisms over opinions, descriptions, or unrelated conditions.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Can I vary one factor, measure the result, and potentially prove this wrong in a simple experiment?”
Use when: The question asks for a hypothesis for an investigation about why a physical change happened.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for an observation, prediction without testing, personal preference, or a noncausal description.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what happens when energy changes form in a physical system, then apply conservation first and reject creation or destruction claims.
Error pattern: Success came from using a core law instead of tracking the specific forms too literally.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “In this scenario, is energy only transformed or also entering/leaving the system?” If only transformed, total stays unchanged.
Use when: Relevant in science items about conversions among chemical, mechanical, thermal, electrical, light, or sound energy.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt concerns open-system accounting, efficiency losses across boundaries, or asks about one specific form rather than total energy.

Transfer rule: If equipment is described as reflective or shiny, then infer its main function is reducing radiant heat/light absorption rather than blocking pressure loss or impacts.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a material property to the physical hazard it directly mitigates: reflection addresses radiation exposure.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this feature primarily affect radiation, mechanical penetration, or containment?” and choose the hazard altered by reflection.
Use when: Apply this on questions linking clothing, coatings, or surfaces to environmental protection, especially in high-light or high-heat settings.
Boundary: Ignore this when the feature named is thickness, airtight sealing, puncture resistance, or multilayer structure, which point to different hazards.

Transfer rule: If a question can be tested by students with a controlled classroom experiment and measurable outcomes, then select it.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing directly investigable variables from broad facts needing remote observation or large-scale data.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Can I assign conditions, keep most factors constant, collect observations in class, and compare results within days or weeks?”
Use when: The options mix hands-on experimental questions with questions about distant places, global extremes, or long-range animal behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks about research methods beyond class investigations, such as surveys, field expeditions, or astronomy datasets.

Transfer rule: If a safety question involves electrical equipment, then prioritize choices that reduce conductivity and shock risk in the environment.
Error pattern: Successful pattern—matched the main hazard mechanism to the option instead of picking generic protective behavior.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, name the primary injury pathway; if water or moisture increases that risk, prefer the option that removes moisture exposure.
Use when: Apply for multiple-choice safety items about powered tools, appliances, outlets, cords, or any device using electricity.
Boundary: Ignore when the question targets a different hazard source, a specific procedure, or required gear explicitly stated by the scenario.

Transfer rule: If an environmental event changes several habitat factors, then select the option that directly lowers survival or reproduction resources.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each effect by whether it reduces or improves key needs rather than reacting to the disaster word alone.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does this make food, nesting, safety, or predator pressure better or worse for the species, and mark only true harms.
Use when: Apply this on ecology questions about population impacts, habitat disturbance, disasters, or resource changes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for indirect effects, long-term tradeoffs, or impacts on another species instead of the focal population.

Transfer rule: If asked how to decrease daily trash output, then choose the action that reduces waste generation or diverts reusable material from disposal.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the goal to the only option that changes the waste stream, not merely its location or quantity.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does this lower what gets discarded per person, or just move it, add to it, or clean it up afterward?
Use when: Apply this on environmental or habits questions about reducing waste, pollution, or resource use through individual actions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about disposal methods, litter cleanup, or immediate sanitation rather than reducing total discarded material.

Transfer rule: If a claim is about energy release in a reaction, then choose evidence that directly shows heat or light being produced.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the conclusion’s variable to an observable indicator rather than picking unrelated descriptive data.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this evidence visibly or quantitatively demonstrate the claimed property itself, not just the setup, amounts, or timing?”
Use when: Apply to questions asking which evidence best supports a scientific conclusion, especially about reaction type, energy change, or validity of an inference.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim concerns identity, conservation, rate, or yield, where direct energy indicators are not the target evidence.

Transfer rule: If choices mix innate animal behaviors with an ability improved through learning/practice, then pick the learned skill as not instinct.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized and treated any common animal behavior as automatic, ignoring the instinct-versus-acquired distinction.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can an animal perform this correctly the first time without being taught or practicing?” Eliminate those that are yes.
Use when: This applies to biology or behavior questions asking whether an action is innate, inherited, automatic, or instead learned.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns exceptions, species-specific facts, or behaviors explicitly defined as partly instinctive and partly learned.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a benefit, then choose the option stating a clear advantage or useful outcome, not a neutral trait or drawback.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by valence and function: benefit versus cost, difficulty, or ordinary feature.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this help users or improve performance?” Eliminate any choice that is merely descriptive or negative.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items asking for an advantage, purpose, helpful effect, or positive feature of an object or activity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a fact regardless of value, or when a neutral characteristic is explicitly requested.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a drawback of an information source, then test each choice for whether it is inherently negative rather than beneficial or neutral.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying options by valence and source reliability instead of being distracted by common features.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label every option as advantage, disadvantage, or context-dependent; choose only an option that directly matches the asked problem type.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items about evaluating sources, media, tools, or methods by strengths versus weaknesses.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a benefit, a factual property, or a tradeoff requiring domain-specific evidence.

Transfer rule: If choices compare a celestial body to Earth, then verify each option against basic properties: solidity, gravity, atmosphere, and sunlight.
Error pattern: Success came from eliminating absolute or physically impossible claims and selecting the scientifically supported distinguishing trait.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Is this universally false because the body clearly exists physically, exerts/feels gravity, or is illuminated by the Sun?”
Use when: Apply on elementary astronomy questions about comparing planets, moons, or other bodies using common physical characteristics.
Boundary: Ignore when the question depends on detailed measurements, exceptions, or specialized phenomena beyond basic observable properties.

Transfer rule: If choices involve different Earth systems, then pick the method with the smallest direct ground disturbance for the lithosphere.
Error pattern: Success came from matching each activity to its primary physical impact rather than to general environmental harm.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it excavate, drill, remove subsurface material, or mainly affect living cover while leaving rock/soil structure mostly intact?
Use when: Apply this on environmental science questions comparing resource extraction methods by impact on a specific sphere such as rock, soil, air, water, or biosphere.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about total ecological damage, long-term pollution, or impacts outside the named Earth sphere.

Transfer rule: If a question asks the main advantage of teamwork over individual work, then choose the option about combining and sharing ideas, skills, or perspectives.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on the defining benefit of collaboration rather than side effects like time, cost, or recognition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Would this benefit exist specifically because multiple people interact?” If not, reject it.
Use when: Apply this on school or workplace items comparing group work with solo work and asking for the primary benefit.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about a special case, a documented outcome, or a disadvantage/tradeoff of teamwork.

Transfer rule: If a star-like body becomes larger or more energetic, then place a potentially habitable planet farther away to keep received energy in a life-supporting range.
Error pattern: Success came from using a causal habitability model: source output changes imply orbital-distance adjustment, not planet-size adjustment.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option directly changes incoming energy at the planet in the compensating direction?”
Use when: Apply this to astronomy or climate-habitability questions involving changes in a central energy source and what must shift to preserve similar conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question centers on gravity, composition, atmosphere, tides, or explicitly says luminosity does not track size.

Transfer rule: If a food’s main macronutrient is protein, then expect digestion to break it down mostly into amino acids.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the digestion product to the dominant macronutrient rather than the food’s category or appearance.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option by dominant macronutrient—protein, carbohydrate, or fat—and choose only an option whose primary component is protein.
Use when: This applies to digestion, biomolecule, enzyme, or nutrient-product questions involving whole foods or food groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are purified mixtures, fortified foods, or the question asks about minor components, not the main breakdown product.

Transfer rule: If a trait resemblance question asks for the biological cause, then choose inherited genetic information over shared environment or behavior.
Error pattern: Success came from separating heredity mechanisms from learned, cultural, or lifestyle similarities.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as inherited at conception versus acquired after birth; prefer the inherited mechanism.
Use when: Apply this to questions about why offspring physically resemble parents or share innate biological traits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about habits, skills, language, preferences, or other traits mainly shaped by environment.

Transfer rule: If comparing Earth with an airless body, then verify which listed features are actual shared landforms rather than climate, liquids, or gases.
Error pattern: Chose by loose association and ignored basic physical prerequisites; failed to eliminate options requiring atmosphere or liquid bodies.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does the other body physically possess this feature now? Cross out anything needing weather, breathable gas, or open water.
Use when: Relevant in astronomy or Earth science questions that compare planets, moons, or surfaces using broad physical-feature categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about ancient conditions, metaphorical wording, or hidden definitions beyond visible physical geography.

Transfer rule: If two substances are physically mixed but remain chemically unchanged and visibly separate into phases, then choose the option for a heterogeneous mixture, not a new substance or state.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by mixing behavior and phase separation instead of by ingredients alone.
Diagnostic check: Ask: after stirring, do the components merge uniformly, or do droplets/layers reappear with time and no reaction signs?
Use when: Apply this to questions about combining materials and deciding between pure substance, compound, solution, or heterogeneous mixture.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt describes chemical bonding, heat/light production, gas formation, or a single uniform phase.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what changes after a magnetic-field reversal, then choose effects tied to magnetic recording or compass orientation, not orbital, seasonal, or rotational mechanics.
Error pattern: Success came from linking the cause to the directly governed physical property instead of unrelated Earth-system processes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the phenomenon controlled by the field and verify the option changes sign/orientation with polarity while the others would remain unchanged.
Use when: Apply this on geoscience items about magnetism, seafloor formation, remanent signatures, or polarity changes in newly created material.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question involves climate cycles, tectonic generation itself, or axial spin changes without magnetic evidence.

Transfer rule: If a quantity asks for velocity, then choose the option that includes both distance-per-time units and a direction.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking all defining components, not matching on a familiar number or unit alone.
Diagnostic check: Underline two required features—rate unit and direction—and verify the chosen option explicitly contains both.
Use when: Apply this on motion or vector-vs-scalar questions where answer choices vary by units, magnitude, and directional wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the quantity sought is scalar only, or direction is irrelevant or already fixed by the problem statement.

Transfer rule: If a biology question asks for the broad role of sexual reproduction, then choose the function tied to producing offspring and maintaining the species, not guaranteed similarity or population growth.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on the core biological purpose rather than tempting absolute claims about appearance, identity, or long-term numbers.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, eliminate any option with words like “all,” “identical,” or guaranteed increase; keep the one describing reproduction’s species-level function.
Use when: Apply this to life-science items about reproduction, inheritance, or population outcomes in plants and animals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about a specific mechanism, genetic variation details, or asexual reproduction.

Transfer rule: If choices mix elements, mixtures, and pure substances, then select the one made of different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying matter by type instead of relying on familiar names or everyday usage.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: one element only, bonded combination with a constant formula, or physical blend with variable composition?
Use when: This applies to science questions asking to distinguish compounds from elements, mixtures, solutions, or common household materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task concerns reactions, properties, or naming details rather than identifying matter type.

Transfer rule: If comparing traits within one species, then choose the inherited species-level trait, not size or count traits shaped by age or environment.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating identity-defining characteristics from developmental or environmental variation among individuals.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would two healthy individuals of the same species commonly differ in this trait without mutation? Reject traits that change with growth, season, or conditions.
Use when: Relevant in biology questions about variation among members of one species or population.
Boundary: Ignore when the question compares different species, cultivars, sexes, life stages, or explicitly mentions mutations or abnormalities.

Transfer rule: If a separator uses magnetism, then choose the mixture where one component is ferromagnetic and the other is not.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each material by magnetic response instead of surface appearance or everyday use.
Diagnostic check: For each component, ask “Is it strongly attracted to a magnet?”; accept only if exactly one gets a clear yes.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice questions about separating mixtures by a physical tool or property, especially magnets.
Boundary: Ignore when separation depends on other properties, or when materials are both magnetic, both nonmagnetic, or only weakly magnetic.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the major limitation of automation, then prefer the constraint that blocks flexible use across many settings, not ordinary operating needs.
Error pattern: I overvalued a universal maintenance requirement instead of identifying the deeper dependence on stable, unchanging conditions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this merely describe any machine, or does it uniquely restrict where automation can reliably replace people?
Use when: Apply this on questions about advantages, limits, or suitability of machines, robots, or automated systems in production tasks.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is specifically about upkeep costs, power supply, or mechanical failures rather than core deployment constraints.

Transfer rule: If a natural-selection prompt asks what “fitness” means, then choose the trait tied to leaving more viable, fertile offspring, not mere strength or survival.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping evolutionary terms to reproductive output rather than to toughness, food intake, or mutation-related mechanisms.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this factor directly increase the number of descendants in the next generation?” If not, reject it.
Use when: Apply for biology items about fitness, adaptation, selection, or interpretations of common evolutionary phrases.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is instead about causes of variation, immediate survival only, physiology, or environmental resources without inheritance.

Transfer rule: If a substance changes from liquid to solid, then choose the option pairing decreased particle kinetic energy with particles becoming more closely packed.
Error pattern: Success comes from linking state change to both energy change and spacing change, instead of focusing on only one property.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does freezing mean particles slow down, and in this case does the solid occupy less space than the liquid?”
Use when: Apply on phase-change questions that ask how particle motion and spacing change during cooling or freezing.
Boundary: Ignore when the material is an exception whose solid is less dense than its liquid, or when temperature is held constant during the phase change.

Transfer rule: If an ecosystem question asks for the most likely drought effect, then trace the immediate resource shortage from water loss to food decline to organism movement.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing direct ecological consequences over tempting but less universal physiological or long-term process claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rank options by immediacy and generality: water availability, plant productivity, consumer survival, movement, then eliminate effects not broadly caused by drought.
Use when: Apply this on ecology items about abiotic stress, especially drought, scarcity, population response, and short-term ecosystem impacts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets a specific species physiology, long-term community change, or experimental data showing an unusual response.

Transfer rule: If land-use change removes large areas of living plants, then first predict less photosynthesis, not less combustion-related emissions.
Error pattern: I focused on one carbon-effect pathway and ignored the direct atmospheric role of the removed organisms.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list what the removed biomass normally takes in and releases; then infer which atmospheric process immediately drops.
Use when: Apply this to questions about deforestation, crop conversion, habitat clearing, or loss of photosynthetic biomass affecting air composition.
Boundary: Ignore this when the scenario centers on added technology, chemical scrubbing, or nonbiological atmospheric processes rather than plant removal.

Transfer rule: If choices compare force and mass, then compute acceleration as force divided by mass for each choice before selecting.
Error pattern: Success came from using the governing ratio instead of comparing force or mass alone.
Diagnostic check: For every option, write a quick force-to-mass quotient and confirm the largest quotient matches your choice.
Use when: Apply this on mechanics questions asking which object speeds up most under different applied forces and masses.
Boundary: Ignore this when acceleration depends on additional factors like friction, angled forces, changing mass, or nonconstant net force.

Transfer rule: If an object moves with constant velocity in a straight line, then choose the description stating the net force is zero and forces are balanced.
Error pattern: Success came from applying Newton’s first law instead of matching force direction to motion direction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is speed changing or direction changing?” If neither changes, infer zero acceleration and zero net force.
Use when: Apply this on motion/forces questions involving steady speed, unchanged direction, equilibrium, or net-force reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore this when there is any acceleration, turning, friction change, or the question asks about a single force rather than the net force.

Transfer rule: If a phase-change question asks where water absorbs energy, then choose transitions into higher-energy, less-ordered states.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying processes by energy direction instead of matching familiar water-cycle vocabulary.
Diagnostic check: For each listed process, ask whether heat must be added or removed; keep only “added” processes.
Use when: Apply this on water-cycle, states-of-matter, or phase-change items that mix liquid, solid, and gas transitions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the process is mechanical movement, mixing, or temperature change without a change of state.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what most benefits users of an identification payment method, then choose the option that most directly improves user safety or privacy in that method.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on the stakeholder’s primary risk, not on side effects that mainly help sellers or speed.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each option as user protection, merchant advantage, convenience, or finance; pick the one uniquely reducing misuse or exposure.
Use when: Apply this on consumer-benefit questions about new payment, biometric, account, or authentication technologies.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly prioritizes price, transaction speed, rewards, or business analytics over user security.

Transfer rule: If asked for a group’s function in a food web, then match it to its core ecological role, not a side effect or another group’s job.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing nutrient recyclers from producers and consumer-level organisms by their defining process.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state what material or energy the group acts on and what output it returns to the ecosystem.
Use when: Apply this for food-web or niche questions involving producers, consumers, scavengers, or organisms that break down dead matter.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about a species-specific interaction, habitat, behavior, or population change rather than trophic role.

Transfer rule: If an energy-source question asks for a “problem,” then evaluate broad environmental and health impacts from extraction, transport, combustion, and waste.
Error pattern: Success came from rejecting distractors that confuse scarcity, low energy yield, or biological contamination with the source’s real hazards.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list 2–3 known byproducts or side effects and ask whether the option matches a well-established consequence.
Use when: Apply this on basic science or environmental questions comparing fuels, power generation methods, or resource tradeoffs.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about cost, efficiency, availability, or a specific technical process rather than harms.

Transfer rule: If a hygiene measure is added in shared spaces, then infer its primary purpose is reducing transmission through touch/contact.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the intervention’s direct mechanism to the health outcome, not to indirect benefits or unrelated goals.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What immediate pathway does this item affect?” Then compare touch spread, airborne spread, resource saving, and behavior guidance.
Use when: The question describes sanitation, cleaning, barriers, or hand-related practices in classrooms, labs, bathrooms, or other shared-use environments.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the measure mainly targets air quality, long-term education, equipment safety, or environmental conservation rather than contact exposure.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the most immediate effect of low water in a cell, then prioritize functions directly dependent on water-driven internal pressure or volume.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the resource deficit to the nearest mechanical consequence, not a slower metabolic or life-cycle effect.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list which option would fail first if water dropped suddenly: shape support, energy capture, gas output, or future division.
Use when: Apply this on biology items about shortages of water and asking what happens first or immediately to a cell.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns long-term consequences, noncellular scales, or another limiting factor is more direct than water.

Transfer rule: If asked for the source of erupted molten rock, then choose the plastic upper-mantle layer beneath tectonic plates, not the rigid surface shell or metallic core.
Error pattern: Confused the trigger/location of volcanism with the reservoir that supplies melt.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option by state and position: rigid plate layer, ductile upper mantle, liquid metal layer, solid metal center; pick the melt-generating rocky layer.
Use when: Relevant for Earth-structure questions about volcanoes, magma origin, mantle convection, or plate-boundary melting.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about where eruptions occur at the surface, plate mechanics alone, or seismic/compositional properties unrelated to magma source.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a familiar chemical formula in atom counts, then translate the formula into subscripts and convert omitted subscripts to 1.
Error pattern: Success came from recalling a standard formula and mapping it correctly to numbers of each atom.
Diagnostic check: Write the formula symbolically, count each element’s subscript, and verify the total atoms match the choice exactly.
Use when: Apply this to basic chemistry items about molecular composition, formulas, or names of common compounds.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task concerns ionic ratios, structural isomers, or properties rather than counting atoms in one molecule.

Transfer rule: If two protists are compared, then match only traits both clearly possess from basic cell biology, not lifestyle or reproduction assumptions.
Error pattern: Overgeneralized a group-specific trait and ignored a shared structural feature visible across both organisms.
Diagnostic check: For each option, say “both, one, or neither” using known structures/functions; eliminate any choice not true for both.
Use when: The question asks for a common characteristic between microorganisms or simple eukaryotes with different nutrition, reproduction, or social organization.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a difference, a unique trait, or when one organism’s identity/features are uncertain.

Transfer rule: If an object moves downward under gravity and speeds up, then infer kinetic energy increases while gravitational potential energy decreases.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking how energy shifts between forms instead of assuming all energies change together.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare start vs. later height and speed; lower height means less gravitational potential, greater speed means more kinetic.
Use when: Apply this to ramps, drops, slides, pendulums, or any motion where gravity changes height and motion.
Boundary: Ignore this when height stays constant, external work dominates, or the question concerns total energy including losses like frictional heating.

Transfer rule: If choices change habitat conditions, then pick the one that most increases a limiting resource required for growth and reproduction.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: compare each option by its net effect on basic survival needs rather than by surface intensity or weather severity alone.
Diagnostic check: For every option, mark whether it raises or lowers access to water, light, suitable temperature, or physical safety; choose the strongest net positive.
Use when: Apply this to ecology questions asking which environmental change will increase or decrease a population size.
Boundary: Ignore this when the species is adapted to unusual conditions, when excess of a resource becomes harmful, or when biotic interactions dominate.

Transfer rule: If an object’s motion or vibration directly produces noise, then classify the source energy as motion-based before the sound output.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the immediate physical cause of the sound rather than picking unrelated common energy forms.
Diagnostic check: Identify what is actively changing right before the sound; if it is movement, impact, or vibration, map input to motion-based energy.
Use when: Apply this on questions about toys, instruments, collisions, shaking, striking, or any action where sound follows visible movement.
